'''Helen Rhoda Arnold Quinn''' (born 19 May 1943) is an Australian-born [[particle physicist]] and educator who has made major contributions to both fields. Her contributions to theoretical physics include the [[Peccei–Quinn theory]] which implies a corresponding symmetry of nature<ref name=PQSym /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/roberto-peccei-and-helen-quinn-driving-around-stanford-in-a-clunky-jeep-20170615/|title=Roberto Peccei and Helen Quinn, Driving Around Stanford in a Clunky Jeep, Quanta Magazine|date=15 June 2021}}</ref>(related to matter-antimatter symmetry and the possible source of the dark matter that pervades the universe) and contributions to the search for a unified theory for the three types of [[Fundamental interaction|particle interactions]] (strong, electromagnetic, and weak). As Chair of the [[Board on Science Education]] of the [[National Academy of Sciences]], Quinn led the effort that produced ''A Framework for K-12 Science Education: Practices, Crosscutting Concepts, and Core Ideas''<ref name="K12Framework">{{Cite book|url=https://www.nap.edu/catalog/13165/a-framework-for-k-12-science-education-practices-crosscutting-concepts|title=A Framework for K-12 Science Education: Practices, Crosscutting Concepts, and Core Ideas|last=Council|first=National Research|date=2011-07-19|isbn=9780309217422|language=en|doi=10.17226/13165}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/helen-quinn-on-physics-and-education-20161018/|title=A Wormhole Between Physics and Education, Quanta Magazine|date=18 October 2016}}</ref>—the basis for the [[Next Generation Science Standards]] adopted by many states. Her honours include the [[Dirac Medal (ICTP)|Dirac Medal of the International Center for Theoretical Physics]], the [[Oskar Klein Medal]] from the [[Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences]], appointment as an Honorary Officer of the [[Order of Australia]], the J. J. [[Sakurai Prize]] for Theoretical Particle Physics from the [[American Physical Society]], the Karl Taylor Compton Medal for Leadership in Physics from the [[American Institute of Physics]], the 2018 [[Benjamin Franklin Medal (Franklin Institute)|Benjamin Franklin Medal]] in Physics from the [[Franklin Institute]], and the 2023 [[Harvey Prize]] from [[Technion -- Israel Institute of Technology]].

==Life==
Quinn grew up in Australia. Of her childhood with her three brothers, she says, "I learned very young how to make myself heard."<ref>{{Cite book |last=Yount |first=Lisa |title=A to Z of Women in Science |publisher=Facts on File, Inc. |year=2008 |isbn=9780816066957 |edition=Revised |location=New York, NY |pages=248}}</ref> She graduated in 1959 from [[Tintern Grammar]], Tintern Church of England Girls' Grammar School,<ref name=CWP /> in Ringwood East, [[Victoria, Australia]]. She began college at the [[University of Melbourne]] before moving to the United States and transferring to [[Stanford University]]. She received her PhD from [[Stanford University|Stanford]] in 1967, at a time when less than 2% of physicists were women. She did her postdoctoral work at the [[DESY]] (the German Synchrotron Laboratory) in Hamburg, Germany. She next spent seven years at [[Harvard University]] before returning to Stanford, where she became a professor of physics in the [[SLAC Theory Group|Theory Group]] at the [[SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory]], then known as the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center. She retired in 2010<ref>{{cite web |url=https://fndeats.files.wordpress.com/2013/03/quinn_symposium_poster.png |title=Poster |website=fndeats.files.wordpress.com}}</ref> and devoted her efforts to education, especially K-12 and preschool science and multilingual education.<ref name="ggstem">{{Cite news|url=https://ggstem.wordpress.com/2013/03/22/helen-quinn/|title=Helen Quinn|date=2013-03-22|work=[[Grandma Got STEM]]|language=en-US}}</ref>

==Professional contributions==
Working with [[Howard Georgi]] and [[Steven Weinberg]], Quinn showed<ref>{{cite journal |first1=H. |last1=Georgi |first2=H.R. |last2=Quinn |first3=S. |last3=Weinberg |title=Hierarchy of interactions in Unified Gauge Theories |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=33 |issue=7 |pages=451–4 |year=1974 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.33.451 |bibcode = 1974PhRvL..33..451G }}</ref> how the three types of [[Fundamental interaction|particle interactions]] (strong, electromagnetic, and weak), which look very different as we see their impact in the world around us, become very similar in extremely high-energy processes and so might be three aspects of a single unified force.

With [[Roberto Peccei]], she originated [[Peccei–Quinn theory]], which suggested a possible near-symmetry of the universe (now known as [[Peccei–Quinn symmetry]])<ref name=PQSym>{{cite journal |author1-link=Roberto Peccei |first1=R.D. |last1=Peccei |first2=H.R. |last2=Quinn |title=CP conservation in the presence of pseudoparticles |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=38 |issue=25 |pages=1440–3 |year=1977 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.38.1440 |bibcode=1977PhRvL..38.1440P }}</ref> to explain how strong interactions can maintain [[CP-symmetry]] (the symmetry between matter and antimatter) when weak interactions do not. One consequence of this theory is a particle known as the [[axion]] which has yet to be observed but is one candidate for the [[dark matter]] that pervades the universe.

She showed how the physics of [[quarks]] can be used to predict certain aspects of the physics of [[hadrons]] (which are particles made from quarks) regardless of the details of the hadron's structure (with [[Enrico Poggio]] and [[Steven Weinberg]]).<ref>{{cite journal |first1=E.C. |last1=Poggio |first2=H.R. |last2=Quinn |first3=S. |last3=Weinberg |title=Smearing method in the quark model |journal=Physical Review D |volume=13 |issue=7 |pages=1958–1968 |year=1976 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.13.1958 |bibcode = 1976PhRvD..13.1958P }}</ref> This useful property is now known as [[quark-hadron duality]].

She has given public talks in various countries on "[[CP violation|The Missing Antimatter]]", in which she suggests that this area of research is promising.

In 2001, she was elected to become president of the [[American Physical Society]] for the year 2004. She was the fourth woman to be elected to the APS presidential line in the Society's 102-year history.<ref name="ApsPres">{{cite web|url=https://www.aps.org/publications/apsnews/200111/quinn.cfm|title=APS Members Elect Helen Quinn as Society's Next Vice President|date=November 2001|website=www.aps.org|access-date=13 September 2017}}</ref>

Quinn has had a long term engagement in education issues.<ref name=CWP /> She was a cofounder and the first president of the [[Contemporary Physics Education Project]], and helped design its first product, the chart of Fundamental Particles and Interactions that appears on many schoolhouse walls next to the periodic table chart. CPEP received the 2017 "Excellence in Physics Education Award" from the American Physical Society, "for leadership in providing educational materials on contemporary physics topics to students for over 25 years."<ref name="CPEPwebsite">{{cite web|url=http://www.cpepPhysics.org|title=Contemporary Physics Education Project - CPEP|website=www.cpepphysics.org|access-date=13 September 2017}}</ref>

She was elected to the [[National Academy of Sciences]] (NAS) while she was a staff member at [[SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory|SLAC]];<ref name="apsnas" /><ref name="web.stanford.edu">{{cite web|url=https://web.stanford.edu/dept/news/pr/03/nas200357.html|title=Seven Stanford faculty elected to National Academy of Sciences|last=Trei|first=Lisa|date=2003-05-05|website=web.stanford.edu|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160614052542/https://web.stanford.edu/dept/news/pr/03/nas200357.html|archive-date=2016-06-14|url-status=dead|access-date=13 September 2017}}</ref> she was soon made a full professor of physics at Stanford. As a member of NAS, she joined the [[Board on Science Education]] of the National Research Council and has served on a number of its studies. She served as chair of this board for the years 2009–2014.

After retiring from Stanford, she spent her full effort on education. She planned and led the work of the NRC study committee that produced ''[[A Framework for K-12 Science Education]]''<ref name=K12Framework /> to guide the development of multi-state standards for science education.  These "[[Next Generation Science Standards]]" were released in final form in April, 2013. NGSS has been officially adopted by many states and the District of Columbia. Since the release of the Framework, she has worked to support the ongoing process of development, adoption, and implementation of the NGSS.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://ell.stanford.edu/leadership|title=Leadership - Understanding Language|website=ell.stanford.edu|access-date=13 September 2017|archive-date=19 May 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120519024100/http://ell.stanford.edu/leadership|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://web.stanford.edu/group/ngss_assessment/cgi-bin/snapgse/?page_id=15|title=Stanford NGSS Assessment Project -|website=web.stanford.edu|access-date=13 September 2017|archive-date=11 November 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151111054751/https://web.stanford.edu/group/ngss_assessment/cgi-bin/snapgse/?page_id=15|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cde.ca.gov/ci/sc/cf/scicfccrecommendedlist.asp|title=Science CFCC Approved Applicants - Curriculum Frameworks (CA Dept of Education)|website=www.cde.ca.gov|access-date=13 September 2017|archive-date=21 October 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141021215417/http://www.cde.ca.gov/ci/sc/cf/scicfccrecommendedlist.asp|url-status=dead}}</ref> With Okhee Lee and Guadalupe Valdez, she studied the opportunities for teaching English to English language learners in the context of NGSS.<ref name="ell">{{cite web|url=http://ell.stanford.edu/publication/language-demands-and-opportunities-relation-next-generation-science-standards-ells|title=Language Demands and Opportunities in Relation to Next Generation Science Standards for ELLs - Understanding Language|last1=Quinn|first1=Helen|last2=Lee|first2=Okhee|website=ell.stanford.edu|access-date=13 September 2017|last3=Valdés|first3=Guadalupe|archive-date=8 December 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121208052313/http://ell.stanford.edu/publication/language-demands-and-opportunities-relation-next-generation-science-standards-ells|url-status=dead}}</ref>

In 2015, the President of [[Ecuador]] appointed her as a member of the board (Comision Gestora) charged with leading the new National University of Education.<ref name=UNAE />

*1972–75 Assistant Professor of Physics, Harvard University
*1976–77 Associate Professor of Physics, Harvard University
*1977–78 Visiting Associate Professor, [[Stanford University]]
*1978–79 Research Associate, SLAC, Stanford University
*1979–2003 Member, Scientific Staff, SLAC, Stanford University
*1988–2004 Education and Public Outreach Manager, SLAC, Stanford University
*1988–2004 Cofounder and first president of the [[Contemporary Physics Education Project]] (CPEP)

Lee Historical Lecture in Physics, Harvard University. Wednesday, November 17, 2021|language=en}}</ref>

Robert Oppenheimer Lecture, [[University of California, Berkeley]]: "Teaching for Learning: What I have learned from learning research".<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://physics.berkeley.edu/news-events/events/20190313/2019-oppenheimer-lecture-teaching-for-learning |title=2019 Oppenheimer Lecture: Teaching for Learning. Wednesday, March 13, 2019 |language=en |access-date=23 June 2020 |archive-date=23 June 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200623113351/https://physics.berkeley.edu/news-events/events/20190313/2019-oppenheimer-lecture-teaching-for-learning |url-status=dead }}</ref> A video of this lecture is available.<ref>{{cite web |title=2019 Oppenheimer Lecture: Teaching for Learning |date=2019 |publisher=[[University of California, Berkeley]] |url=https://physics.berkeley.edu/resources/public-lecture-videos/2019-oppenhiemer-lecture-teaching-for-learning-3041 |access-date=23 June 2020 |archive-date=25 June 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200625215509/https://physics.berkeley.edu/resources/public-lecture-videos/2019-oppenhiemer-lecture-teaching-for-learning-3041 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

* 2018 Awarded the 2018 [[Benjamin Franklin Medal (Franklin Institute)|Benjamin Franklin Medal]] in Physics of the [[Franklin Institute]], "for her pioneering contributions to the long-term quest for a unified theory of the strong, weak, and electromagnetic interactions of fundamental particles."<ref name="Helen Rhoda Quinn">{{Cite news|url=https://www.fi.edu/laureates/helen-rhoda-quinn|title=Helen Rhoda Quinn|date=2017-11-02|work=The Franklin Institute|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web | url=https://www6.slac.stanford.edu/news/2017-11-13-slacs-helen-quinn-honored-2018-benjamin-franklin-medal-physics.aspx | title=SLAC's Helen Quinn Honored with 2018 Benjamin Franklin Medal in Physics}}</ref>
* 2017 Selected to give the annual Dirac Lecture at Cambridge University, sponsored jointly by St John's College and the Department of Applied Mathematics and Theoretical Physics of the University of Cambridge. Her topic: "Antimatter: Dirac's incredible prediction and its consequences." She was the first woman scientist to be selected since the lecture series was begun in 1986.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.talks.cam.ac.uk/talk/index/72485|title=talks.cam : Antimatter: Dirac's incredible prediction and its consequences|date=2017-05-09|website=www.talks.cam.ac.uk|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.joh.cam.ac.uk/annual-lectures#three|title=Distinguished Lecture Series {{!}} StJohns|website=www.joh.cam.ac.uk|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130706002737/http://www.joh.cam.ac.uk/annual-lectures#three|archive-date=2013-07-06|url-status=dead}}</ref>
* 2017 Inducted to the "Avenue of Excellence" at [[Tintern Grammar]], in the first class of inductees. The "Avenue of Excellence" on the Tintern campus honors Tintern graduates, and aims to inspire current and future students to pursue excellence.<ref>{{Cite web | url=https://www.tintern.vic.edu.au/community/avenue-of-excellence/ |title = Avenue of Excellence| date=27 November 2017 }}</ref>
* 2016 [[Karl Taylor Compton Medal]] for Leadership in Physics from the [[American Institute of Physics]] "for her leadership in promoting K-12 education and outreach, including the development of standards and approaches to science education that have had an enormous influence at the local, state, national and international levels, and for her broad and deep contributions to the advancement of theoretical particle physics."<ref name="ApsBio" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www6.slac.stanford.edu/news/2015-11-17-slac%E2%80%99s-helen-quinn-receive-2016-compton-medal.aspx|title=SLAC's Helen Quinn to Receive 2016 Compton Medal|date=2015-11-17|website=slac.stanford.edu}}</ref>

* 2013 [[Sakurai Prize|J. J. Sakurai Prize]] for Theoretical Particle Physics from the [[American Physical Society]] (With Roberto Peccei): "For their proposal of the elegant mechanism to resolve the famous problem of strong-CP violation which, in turn, led to the invention of axions, a subject of intense experimental and theoretical investigation for more than three decades."<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Quinn&first_nm=Helen&year=2013|title=Prize Recipient|website=www.aps.org|access-date=13 September 2017}}</ref>
* 2008 [[Oskar Klein Memorial Lecture|Oskar Klein Medal]] from the [[Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://okc.albanova.se/okmemorial/lecturers/ |title=Lectures - the Oskar Klein Centre |access-date=29 January 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170525225002/http://okc.albanova.se/okmemorial/lecturers/ |archive-date=25 May 2017 |url-status=dead}}</ref> She was the first woman to receive this award.
* 2005 appointed an Honorary Officer of the [[Order of Australia]], "for service to scientific research in the field of theoretical physics and to education" (the award was honorary because Quinn was no longer an Australian citizen)<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://today.slac.stanford.edu/a/2007/11-07.htm|title=Helen Quinn Receives Australian Honor for Outstanding Achievement|last=Tuttle|first=Kelen|date=2007-11-07|website=today.slac.stanford.edu|access-date=23 May 2017|archive-date=8 September 2008|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080908063312/http://today.slac.stanford.edu/a/2007/11-07.htm|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://honours.pmc.gov.au/honours/awards/1129367|title=It's an Honour - Honours - Search Australian Honours|website=www.itsanhonour.gov.au|access-date=28 January 2011|archive-date=2 April 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402112753/http://www.itsanhonour.gov.au/honours/honour_roll/search.cfm?aus_award_id=1129367&search_type=simple&showInd=true|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.navy.gov.au/hmas-sydney-iv-part-3|title=HMAS Sydney (IV) - Part 3|last=Navy|first=Royal Australian|website=www.navy.gov.au|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web | url=http://www.cpepweb.org/order_australia.html | title=CPEP - Contemporary Physics Education Project - CPEP | access-date=25 April 2018 | archive-date=9 May 2008 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080509062329/http://www.cpepweb.org/order_australia.html | url-status=dead }}</ref>
